thread.title: Townie Homes creates affordable housing for Ann Arbor workforce
thread.title_full: Townie Homes creates affordable housing for Ann Arbor workforce

author: Aliana Ritter, Sarayu Bongale
title: Townie Homes creates affordable housing for Ann Arbor workforce
text:
The average price of a single-family home in Ann Arbor is more than $600,000, facing a 3% increase between 2025 and 2026. Townie Homes, an initiative by the Ann Arbor Community Land Trust, aims to create affordable homes for Ann Arbor’s critical workers. Townie Homes are newly built, 2-3 bedroom single family homes priced roughly between $125,000 and $300,000 — much below the average market rate. The program budget currently subsidizes development of 26 homes which are projected to complete construction by the end of the year.
In an interview with The Michigan Daily, Sarah Lorenz, A2CLT founder and executive director, explained that Townie Homes provides essential affordable housing options in Ann Arbor amid rising housing costs. Lorenz said the program keeps homes affordable through the community land trust model which adds deed and pricing restrictions for homeowners when listing their homes on the market.
“The Community Land Trust has a deed restriction or a ground lease that requires people to sell at a similarly low price,” Lorenz said. “They get some appreciation over time, but they’re going to sell it to us at a price that was similar to what they bought at that time. That was the first element (of Townie Homes), because we knew the demand was so great that just us building 100 or 200 homes wasn’t going to bring down the prices of every other house in Ann Arbor.”
In addition, A2CLT utilizes Ann Arbor’s Accessory Dwelling Unit policy, which allows two homes to be built on one parcel of land in certain parts of the city. Lorenz said this splits fees and can also lower home prices.
“We could split the cost of the parcel and the cost of the utilities and fees between two homes,” Lorenz said “That was really crucial to our affordability, and I found that on average, by building two homes on one parcel, we’re able to lower the price of each home by almost $100,000.”
After establishing the deed restriction, A2CLT started looking for land on which to build small projects. Lorenz said A2CLT was able to fund the construction of homes through Tax Increment Financing. Ann Arbor’s TIF plan%20is,of%20a%20person%20or%20corporation.) diverts a portion of tax revenue into subsidies towards infrastructure projects and affordable housing initiatives, like the Townie Homes.
“The great thing is that every single time we build on a vacant parcel, we can get that subsidy if the city and the county approve it,” Lorenz said. “That means we can repeat this over and over again, whereas with grants, there are a very limited number of grant funds available, and so that would have really constrained us. With tax increment financing, it opens up a huge possibility for us to scale this approach.”
In an interview with The Daily, Noah Jaworski, a Townie Home buyer, said the program provided an affordable real estate solution for his family.
“Based on the current housing situation kind of just everywhere, it seems like it’s so hard for any of our friends or other people to purchase houses,” Jaworski said. “Let alone in an area as nice — but also not the most consumer friendly — as Ann Arbor. I couldn’t imagine any other way that we’d be able to realistically afford a home without this.”
In an interview with The Daily, Sophie Jaworski, who purchased a Townie Home with her husband Noah, said the proximity of the home to her workplace and other Ann Arbor destinations reduces transportation costs.
“For me, I work within one mile of two of the different lots, and I think that a lot of the houses that were more affordable for us and our budget were farther away on the opposite side of town,” Sophie Jaworski said. “Our goal is to eliminate using two of our cars. Being walkable to things in the community is important, too.”
Townie Homes are listed and labeled as such across a variety of real estate platforms, such as Zillow and Redfin. Lorenz said with more than 900 people on the Buyer List, A2CLT chooses buyers through a lottery system that prioritizes buyers who qualify as essential to the Ann Arbor workforce.
“What we’re calling our priority buyers would be people who work for organizations — what we call anchor institutions — that enable the city to exist,” Lorenz said. “Those would be city and county employees, first responders like police, fire, EMS, our schools, day care and early childhood, and there’s the Ann Arbor District Library. The almost 30,000 employees who work for the University and may not be able to afford to live here or to buy a home here are our priority buyers.”
In an interview with The Daily, Rackham student Isaac Mier, founder and CEO of Tenant Exchange — an organization allowing renters to review on apartments in Ann Arbor based on various metrics — said he believes the program’s lottery system and resale price restriction limits its effectiveness as a lasting solution to Ann Arbor’s housing challenges.
“The lottery is one of those thorny things where we work the same job and I end up with a home and you don’t, and that’s not a permanent solution to me,” Mier said. “The people that win the lottery are still buying the home, but they don’t really own it in the sense that they can’t sell it at fair market value. They sell it out of marginal increase based on Townie Homes. It’s almost like a fake equity — in a way — that you have from an economic standpoint.”
In an interview with the Daily, Melissa Gall, Michigan Medicine researcher and Townie Home buyer, said that since A2CLT can only build a limited number of homes, a lottery system is the fairest way to give people the opportunity to purchase one.
“If there was more possibility for A2CLT to make more homes, and they didn’t have to use a lottery system that would be better,” Gall said. “But, I think that this is the fairest way.”
Gall told The Daily the program not only offers affordability, but also community.
“I think that forming a community is also a benefit,” Gall said. “We’ve been talking about things like community gardens. Forming those connections, building that community and then also the location is a huge perk for me, and I think people in situations like me who are just looking to be able to live in the community that they work in and build connections with the community.”
Daily Staff Reporters Aliana Ritter and Sarayu Bongale can be reached at alianar@umich.edu and sarayub@umich.edu.
